tweets: A grocer's son from a flooded Bengal village cracked a puzzle astronomers couldn't solve: how do you read a star's temperature from its light alone?

His name was Meghnad Saha, born 6 October 1893 in Dhaka. Too poor for school fees at first, he still clawed his way to Presidency College, Calcutta -- among the sharpest physics minds in colonial India.

In 1920, Saha published an equation linking a star's ionization state to its temperature and pressure. It explained WHY stars show different spectral lines -- the missing physics behind the entire stellar classification system.

The Saha equation became a pillar of modern astrophysics, still used to decode starlight and work out what distant stars are made of. In 1927 he was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society -- rare for an Indian scientist under colonial rule.

Saha went on to found what's now the Saha Institute of Nuclear Physics in Calcutta, and was nominated for the Nobel Prize in Physics more than once. A grocer's son taught the world how to read the stars. Follow @yddoseOfHistory for your daily dose of history.
